items.title: Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets
items.content:
This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

What makes a robot asset SimReady?

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

  • Profile: a group of features for a use case, such as a robot body.
  • Features: capabilities needed for the use case, such as joints that can be controlled.
  • Requirements: checks on the settings needed for each feature, such as a joint’s drive settings.

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

What comes with the asset, and what do you add?

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

What should you check before running a pick-and-place task?

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

  • Joint settings: Review the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings.
  • Movement: Test a small arm movement and open and close the gripper.
  • Contact: Confirm that the can rests on the work surface without falling through it.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

Build a pick-and-place simulation in Isaac Sim

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Required Software:

  • Install Isaac Sim 6.2, the version used for this example, and check its system requirements.
  • Set up an agent of your choice that can use the Isaac Sim skills. Follow the Agent Skills documentation to make the bundled skills available to your agent.
  • Install the Hugging Face CLI only if you choose the command-line asset download option.
  • Use the USD Search endpoint.

Step 1: Download the robot arm, gripper, and beverage can assets

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

~/ASSETS/hf/src/simready-assets-c7fa7615/Robotiq_2F_140/simready_usd/Robotiq_2F_140.usda

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

What does asset validation tell you?

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

Step 2: Assemble the robot and compose the scene for pick and place

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

./isaac-sim.sh --enable isaacsim.code_editor.python_server

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

Sample prompt used in this example:

Assemble the robot arm <local path to Simready ur17g robot usd>
with the gripper <local path to downloded simready Robotiq_2F_140 gripper usd>
using the Robot Assembly tutorial in Isaac Sim
https://docs.isaacsim.omniverse.nvidia.com/6.2.0/robot_setup/assemble_robots.html.

Validate the assembly on completion.

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Step 3: Test the controls and run pick-and-place

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Sample prompt used in this example:

Run pick and place with the assembled robot and soda can
<path to soda can USD from SimReady library> in Isaac Sim.

Ensure you do a contact based grasp for picking up the can and validate
the accuracy/placement error for the pick and place as well.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

Simulation assumptions:

  • Fixed setup: The can starts at a known position, with an anchored robot and clear, flat workspace. No vision was used and collision checks were limited.
  • Simplified can: Deformation and liquid motion are not modeled, so this example does not test crushing.
  • Scripted grasp and motion: A horizontal grasp uses a 2 N·m drive-effort cap chosen through simulation tests, not calibrated to fingertip forces or recommended by the manufacturer. Contact and friction hold the beverage can as the arm follows fixed waypoints without replanning. For hardware gripping-force specifications, see the Robotiq product sheet.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your next simulation with SimReady Assets

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

Discover assets

  • Find robots and objects: Browse SimReady Central on Hugging Face.
  • Check what an asset supports: Review the profiles and requirements in SimReady Foundation alongside the asset’s validation reports.

Build a pick-and-place scene

  • Set up the simulator: Follow the Isaac Sim installation guide for the version used in this example.
  • Connect your agent: Follow the Isaac Sim Agent Skills documentation to make the bundled skills available to your agent.
  • Assemble the robot: Follow the Robot Assembler tutorial if you prefer to connect the arm and gripper manually.

Prepare and contribute content

  • Start from CAD: Follow the 5 Steps to Create SimReady Assets for Robotics to prepare your own robotics assets.
  • Validate and submit assets: Follow the SimReady Central submission guide to make your assets available to other developers.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

What will you build? Share your scene and results in the Hugging Face comments, including the assets and Isaac Sim version you used.

Happy building!

items.title: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question
items.content:
📄 Paper | 🤗 Data | 💻 Code

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

Building XYBench

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

Evaluating how an answer helps

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

  • Pragmatic solution—records whether a model’s response includes solutions to the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X), checking each separately.
  • Pragmatic emphasis—measures whether a model’s answer focuses on the stated request (Y), focuses on the intended request (X), or balances the two.
  • Misconception identification—measures whether a model’s response steers the user toward the underlying goal (X) while discouraging or avoiding the mistaken approach (Y).

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

What the experiments show

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

What this means for evaluation

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

Building XYBench


We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.
For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.




Evaluating how an answer helps


A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.
A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:
Pragmatic solution—records whether a model’s response includes solutions to the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X), checking each separately.
Pragmatic emphasis—measures whether a model’s answer focuses on the stated request (Y), focuses on the intended request (X), or balances the two.
Misconception identification—measures whether a model’s response steers the user toward the underlying goal (X) while discouraging or avoiding the mistaken approach (Y).
In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.
To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.




What the experiments show


We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.
Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.
A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.
A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.





What this means for evaluation


Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.
Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.
We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

Developed with Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins researchers, XYBench includes 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday tasks. The benchmark highlights a critical gap in LLMs' ability to redirect users toward actual solutions, despite often providing relevant but misplaced advice. XYBench aims to help researchers improve AI assistants' troubleshooting skills by recognizing and addressing users' implicit misunderstandings.

items.title: llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem
items.content:
llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

During the 3.5 years since its inception, the project has grown a lot and many downstream applications already depend on our work. We expect this trend to continue as local AI and privacy become increasingly important in our everyday lives. Every new integration means more developers depending on our library interfaces and therefore having a flexible but stable API is paramount.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

Releases

Release Library Public header(s)
llama.cpp v1.0.0 - LLM inference in C/C++ libllama llama.cpp/include/
ggml v1.0.0 - Tensor library for machine learning libggml ggml/include/

Semantic version update rules

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

Change type Bump
MAJOR Breaking change to the public C API in ./include
MINOR Backward-compatible feature, backend updates, model support, or API addition
PATCH Bug fix with no API change

Distribution

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

Channel Platforms
Pre-release artifacts Linux, macOS, Windows, Android, iOS
Docker Linux
Debian Linux
Homebrew macOS, Linux
conda-forge Windows, macOS, Linux
MacPorts macOS
Winget Windows
XCFramework iOS, macOS

Development

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

Backend and model coverage

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

Thanks

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

Additional resources

  • llama.cpp examples
  • ggml-org at Hugging Face
  • ggml-org at Github
  • Check out Llama desktop apps for MacOS and Windows, shipped with love by the team behind llama.cpp and Hugging Face.

items.title: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B
items.content:
LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.     

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

What it enables:

  • Indirect prompt injections, hidden in user data, are mostly ignored by LLMON models due to explicit instruction/data separation. For some benchmarks, attack success rates drop to nearly zero, whereas regular instruction-tuned models get hijacked with high probability. This is achieved while maintaining general capability relative to Granite 4.1 Instruct models.
  • Unrelated passages, old chat turns, and tool outputs don’t get pulled into the answer because each instruction is bound to the exact data it applies to.
  • Instructions, data, and requirements are clearly marked so that their structure and meanings at the application’s code level can be leveraged by the model. Try it out in Mellea, which has native LLMON support enabled by automatically LLMONizing its LLM calls.
  • You no longer need to worry about forcing LLMs to observe JSON structure. Use our converters to turn existing JSON into LLMON without loss. You can also define your own structure and associated tags and tune a LoRA on top of the LLMON models to understand it.

Why not JSON?

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

How is LLMON related to chat templates?

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

messages = [ { "role": "user",
               "instruction": [{ "value": "Write a short paragraph about", "exec": True }],
               "data": [{ "value": "IBM Company", "exec": True }],
               "requirement": [ {"value": "Use less than 10 words", "exec": True},
                                {"value": "Do not use commas", "exec": True}]
             } ]

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

<|open|>instr<|:|>»ñ<|close|>Write a short paragraph about<|open_end|>
<|open|>data<|:|>ä¦<|close|>IBM Company<|open_end|>
<|open|>req<|:|>Á¼<|close|>Use less than 10 words<|open_end|>
<|open|>req<|:|>¢¬<|close|>Do not use commas<|open_end|>
<|open|>exec<|:|>ÄÐ<|close|>
    <|open|>exec<|.|>instruction<|close|>instr<|:|>»ñ<|open_end|>
    <|open|>exec<|.|>input<|close|>data<|:|>ä¦<|open_end|>
    <|open|>exec<|.|>requirement<|close|>req<|:|>Á¼<|open_end|>
    <|open|>exec<|.|>requirement<|close|>req<|:|>¢¬<|open_end|>
    <|open|>exec<|.|>output<|close|>assistant<|:|>ãø<|open_end|>
<|open_end|>
<|open|>assistant<|:|>ãø<|close|>

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

How LLMON addresses prompt injection attacks

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

General capability

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

How we trained the models

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

Bring your own vocabulary (ScienceWorld)

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

Try it today

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

  • Models: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview & granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview
  • Visualization Demo: LLMON Attention Visualization
  • LLMON Repo: https://github.com/generative-computing/llmon
  • Mellea: https://github.com/generative-computing/mellea
  • Papers: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38120, https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.22519

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

You no longer need to worry about forcing LLMs to observe JSON structure. Use our converters to turn existing JSON into LLMON without loss. You can also define your own structure and associated tags and tune a LoRA on top of the LLMON models to understand it.




Why not JSON?


JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.
LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.
Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.




How is LLMON related to chat templates?


LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.
The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.
messages = [ { "role": "user",
               "instruction": [{ "value": "Write a short paragraph about", "exec": True }],
               "data": [{ "value": "IBM Company", "exec": True }],
               "requirement": [ {"value": "Use less than 10 words", "exec": True},
                                {"value": "Do not use commas", "exec": True}]
             } ]

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):
<|open|>instr<|:|>»ñ<|close|>Write a short paragraph about<|open_end|>
<|open|>data<|:|>ä¦<|close|>IBM Company<|open_end|>
<|open|>req<|:|>Á¼<|close|>Use less than 10 words<|open_end|>
<|open|>req<|:|>¢¬<|close|>Do not use commas<|open_end|>
<|open|>exec<|:|>ÄÐ<|close|>
    <|open|>exec<|.|>instruction<|close|>instr<|:|>»ñ<|open_end|>
    <|open|>exec<|.|>input<|close|>data<|:|>ä¦<|open_end|>
    <|open|>exec<|.|>requirement<|close|>req<|:|>Á¼<|open_end|>
    <|open|>exec<|.|>requirement<|close|>req<|:|>¢¬<|open_end|>
    <|open|>exec<|.|>output<|close|>assistant<|:|>ãø<|open_end|>
<|open_end|>
<|open|>assistant<|:|>ãø<|close|>

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.
The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.




How LLMON addresses prompt injection attacks


Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.
We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.




General capability


Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.




How we trained the models


The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.
LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.
The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.





Bring your own vocabulary (ScienceWorld)


LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook. 




Try it today


This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.
Models: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview  & granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview
Visualization Demo: LLMON Attention Visualization
LLMON Repo: https://github.com/generative-computing/llmon
Mellea: https://github.com/generative-computing/mellea
Papers: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38120, https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.22519
Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

summaries.zh: LLMON是一种专为LLM设计的标记语言，旨在解决LLM在处理复杂上下文时因结构隐式或格式不兼容（如JSON）导致的脆性问题。通过使用特殊标记和分隔符，LLMON明确区分指令、数据和约束，有效防止提示注入攻击，并提升模型对上下文的解析能力。目前发布了基于Granite 4.1的3B和8B预览模型，并提供GitHub工具包和示例。与JSON相比，LLMON结构更清晰，更适合LLM处理。它不取代聊天模板，而是通过标记组件含义和关系来丰富模板，实现更精确的指令执行。
summaries.en: LLMON is an LLM-native markup language designed to improve structured communication with large language models (LLMs). It addresses issues like implicit context structures and prompt injections by using explicit tags and special tokens. Two experimental preview models, granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview, are released, along with a GitHub toolkit. LLMON reduces indirect prompt injections, enhances instruction binding, and leverages structure for better model performance. Unlike JSON, LLMON uses reserved tokens for structure, avoiding ambiguity for LLMs. It complements chat templates by adding semantic meaning to components. Conversion tools for JSON are available.

items.title: The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models
items.content:
Update on GitHub

TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository. If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works. Let’s go!

Introduction

3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY. There are also many representations, such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS). Each one has different advantages and disadvantages.

TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format.

The same team then released TRELLIS.2, which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task.

What we want to improve

A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate.

Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task.

Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune.

What will we use?

LoRA

LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide.

Hugging Face Jobs

Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have:

  • A HF_TOKEN that you can obtain from here
  • Your Hugging Face account must have access to DINOv3, because DINOv3 is a gated model
  • If you use your own dataset, upload its meshes to the Hub before you start.

How TRELLIS.2 works

Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters.

TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh.

Encoding the input image

First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object.

Sparse Structure Generation (Sparse Structure Flow)

The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage.

O-Voxel and Structured Latents

O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds.

Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer.

Geometry Generation (Shape Flow)

The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512.

We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape.

Material Generation + Mesh Creation

In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures.

Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file.

Planning

Which components to fine-tune

We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities.

Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training.

If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting.

Why use LoRA

Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more.

What you’ll run

A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning.

To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub:

  1. Give the containers access to your data.
  2. Set the parameters for your task.
  3. Run the preprocessing container.
  4. Run the fine-tuning container.

Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training.

Experiment overview

We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment:

  1. Prepare the data. Convert GLB or OBJ meshes into the latent representations TRELLIS.2 uses for training, and render the input images.
  2. Train the adapters. Run one job for each DiT, with the prepared dataset and a LoRA configuration.
  3. Explain the code. Examine how the containers load the data, add adapters, and train the models.

We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it.

Walkthrough

Running on Hugging Face Jobs

Preprocessing

The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline. See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository. 

export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx  

# Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username

hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large --timeout 6h --secrets HF_TOKEN \
  cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-prep:latest \
  trellis2-prep \
    --meshes your-username/my-meshes \
    --push-to your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \
    --private --holdout 0.05 \
    --views 16 --workers 8

For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments:

flag meaning
-d Detach: print the job ID and URL, then return. To follow the job, run hf jobs logs -f <id>
--flavor a100-large The hardware. We use a100-large (80 GB). To see all options, run hf jobs hardware
--timeout 6h The job stops after this time. Both commands resume. Preprocessing skips finished objects. Training continues from the newest checkpoint in --push-to
--secrets HF_TOKEN Send your token (from HF_TOKEN or hf auth login) to the job as an encrypted environment variable. The token is not written into the image
cr.hf.co/...:latest The image to run. All text after it is the command that runs in the container

This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here. The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later.

LoRA Fine-tuning

The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run.

We use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later.

export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx  # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username

hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large --timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \
  cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \
  trellis2-train --config ss \
    --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \
    --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora \
    --run-name ss_lora \
    --push-path ss_lora \
    --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio

hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large --timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \
  cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \
  trellis2-train --config shape \
    --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \
    --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora \
    --run-name shape_lora \
    --push-path shape_lora \
    --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \
    --set max_steps=3000 i_save=500

If you set --push-to, the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity. A compact script is also available in the same repository.

If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have, feel free to use the following set of commands. 

export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx  

# Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username

# For the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT
hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large --timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \
  cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \
  trellis2-train \
    --config ss \
    --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \
    --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \
    --run-name ss_lora \
    --push-path ss_lora \
    --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \
    --set max_steps=3000 i_save=500

# For the Shape Flow DiT
hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large --timeout 12h --secrets HF_TOKEN \
  cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \
  trellis2-train \
    --config shape \
    --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \
    --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \
    --run-name shape_lora \
    --push-path shape_lora \
    --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \
    --set max_steps=3000 i_save=500

Running locally with Docker

Preprocessing

The commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different. 

# For preprocessing into latents
docker run --gpus all --rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx \
  -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v "$PWD/work":/workspace/work \
  cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-prep:latest \
  trellis2-prep --meshes your-username/my-meshes --push-to your-username/my-meshes-trellis2
LoRA Fine-tuning 
# For Sparse-structure Flow DiT
docker run --gpus all --rm --shm-size 16g \
  -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v "$PWD/work":/workspace/work \
  cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \
  trellis2-train --config ss --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \
    --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio

# For Shape Flow DiT
docker run --gpus all --rm --shm-size 16g \
  -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v "$PWD/work":/workspace/work \
  cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \
  trellis2-train --config shape --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \
    --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio

If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands:

export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx  # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username

# For Sparse-structure Flow DiT
docker run --gpus all --rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN \
  -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \
  -v "$PWD/work":/workspace/work \
  cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \
  trellis2-train \
    --config ss \
    --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \
    --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \
    --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \
    --set max_steps=3000 i_save=500

# For Shape Flow DiT
docker run --gpus all --rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN \
  -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \
  -v "$PWD/work":/workspace/work \
  cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \
  trellis2-train \
    --config shape \
    --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \
    --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \
    --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \
    --set max_steps=3000 i_save=500

Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso

Inside the training pipeline

Preprocessing into latents

We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again.

We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training.

Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object

The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train (ss or shape), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning.

cfg = json.load(
    open(
        {
            "ss": "/workspace/TRELLIS.2/configs/lora/ss_flow_lora_gso.json",
            "shape": "/workspace/TRELLIS.2/configs/lora/slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json",
        }[FLOW]
    )
)

key, latents = {
    "ss": ("ss_latent", "ss_latents/ss_enc_conv3d_16l8_fp16_64"),
    "shape": ("shape_latent", "shape_latents/shape_enc_next_dc_f16c32_fp16_512"),
}[FLOW]


roots = json.dumps(
    {
        "gso": {
            key: f"{DATA}/{latents}",
            "render_cond": f"{DATA}/renders_cond",
            "meta": DATA,
        }
    }
)

ds = getattr(datasets, cfg["dataset"])(roots, **cfg["dataset_args"])

holdout = set(open(f"{DATA}/holdout.txt").read().split())
ds.instances = [(root, sha) for root, sha in ds.instances if sha not in holdout]

batches = cycle(
    DataLoader(
        ds,
        batch_size=BATCH,
        shuffle=True,
        drop_last=True,
        num_workers=4,
        collate_fn=getattr(ds, "collate_fn", None),
    )
)

Preparing LoRA adapters

We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model(). This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface.

We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point (fp32) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 (bf16) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored. 


model = models.from_pretrained(cfg["ckpt"])
for block in model.blocks:
    block.use_checkpoint = True

inject_adapter_in_model(
    LoraConfig(
        r=cfg["rank"], lora_alpha=cfg["alpha"], target_modules=cfg["lora_targets"]
    ),
    model,
)

params = []
for name, p in model.named_parameters():
    p.requires_grad_("lora_" in name)
    if p.requires_grad:
        p.data = p.data.float()  # fp32 master weights for LoRA
        params.append(p)

model.cuda().train()

Training

It’s important to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3, Flux 2, and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching.

We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen.

The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands.

We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images. 

opt = torch.optim.AdamW(
    params, lr=cfg["lr"], weight_decay=cfg["weight_decay"], betas=(0.9, 0.95)
)

dino = DinoV3FeatureExtractor(
    cfg["image_cond_model"], image_size=cfg["image_size"]
).cuda()

We then follow these steps within the training loop:

  • Sample a timestep t for each sample (using logitNormal for the sparse-structure flow DiT and uniform for the shape flow DiT based on the TRELLIS.2 config).
  • Generate random noise matching the data shape and reshape t for broadcasting.
  • Mix clean data with noise based on t (where t = 0 is data with minimal noise, and t = 1 is pure noise).
  • Predict velocity at t × 1000 to match pretraining conditions.
  • Calculate loss as the mean squared error between the predicted velocity and target velocity (the first derivative of x_t).
def flow_loss(x0, cond):
    s = cfg["t_schedule"]

    t = (
        torch.rand(x0.shape[0])
        if s["name"] == "uniform"
        else torch.sigmoid(
            torch.randn(x0.shape[0]) * s["args"]["std"] + s["args"]["mean"]
        )
    )
    t = t.cuda()

    noise = (
        x0.replace(torch.randn_like(x0.feats))
        if cfg["sparse"]
        else torch.randn_like(x0)
    )

    tv = t.view(-1, *[1] * (len(x0.shape) - 1))

    x_t = (1 - tv) * x0 + (cfg["sigma_min"] + (1 - cfg["sigma_min"]) * tv) * noise

    pred, target = model(x_t, t * 1000, cond), (1 - cfg["sigma_min"]) * noise - x0

    return (
        F.mse_loss(pred.feats, target.feats)
        if cfg["sparse"]
        else F.mse_loss(pred, target)
    )

The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches.

For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps.


for step in range(1, STEPS + 1):
    for _ in range(ACCUM):
        batch = next(batches)
        x0 = recursive_to_device(batch["x_0"], "cuda")

        with torch.no_grad():
            cond = dino(batch["cond"])
            cond[torch.rand(len(cond), device="cuda") < cfg["p_uncond"]] = 0

        with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
            loss = flow_loss(x0, cond) / ACCUM

            loss.backward()

    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, cfg["grad_clip"])

    opt.step()
    opt.zero_grad()

Results

We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours.

The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry.

Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects.

The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans.

We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set:

Metric What it means
Chamfer distance The distance from points on one surface to the nearest points on the other surface, measured in both directions. Lower is better.
F-score @ 0.02 The combination of precision (how much of the generated surface is near the reference) and recall (how much of the reference surface the generated surface covers). Here, the matching threshold is 2% of the scan’s bounding-box diagonal. Higher is better.
Normal consistency How closely the surface directions agree. A surface normal is a vector perpendicular to the surface. Higher is better.

In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects.

For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space.

Future directions

Phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate jobs, and evaluated the outputs on held-out objects.

The main lesson is to select a training target that agrees with the problem and the data that you have. For this experiment, we fine-tuned the structure and shape stages and froze the texture stage.

Next, we can examine if the same choices help other 3D generation models, such as Pixal3D and UniLat3D.

Gaussian-splat and world-generation models, such as HunyuanWorld 2.0 and NVIDIA Lyra 2.0, are also possible next steps. Their representations and training pipelines can need different methods.

Thank you for following along, and see you in the next one! 👋🤗
