items.title: A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.
items.content:
Update on GitHub

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Why a voice should live on your device

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

What we released

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

Demos and first projects

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

How Phonon did on the Hugging Face Open TTS Leaderboard

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

Inference

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

from transformers import AutoProcessor, GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration

model_id = "gradium/phonon-31m-en"
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto")
model = GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto")

print(f"{model.num_parameters():,}")  # 30,788,354
print(f"{processor.audio_tokenizer.num_parameters():,}")  # 10,305,313

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from safetensors.torch import load_file

path = hf_hub_download("gradium/phonon-voices", "voices/LMDIYE0Oa377Qh6Z.safetensors")
voice = load_file(path)["speaker_wavs"][0].T  # (num_frames, 512)

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

conversation = [
    {"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "audio"}, {"type": "text", "text": "Hello from Phonon."}]}
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    conversation,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    processor_kwargs={"audio_prompt_latents": [voice]},
).to(model.device)
# prompt: <|audio_prompt|> × num_frames, "Hello from Phonon.", <|audio_bos|>

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

outputs = model.generate(**inputs)  # audio_latents: (batch_size, num_frames, 32)
audio = processor.decode(outputs.audio_latents, outputs.audio_latents_mask)
processor.save_audio(audio, "phonon.wav")

See the docs 🤗 for more!

What's next

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.
On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.
Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.





Inference


We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).
Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.
It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.
Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:
from transformers import AutoProcessor, GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration

model_id = "gradium/phonon-31m-en"
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto")
model = GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto")

print(f"{model.num_parameters():,}")  # 30,788,354
print(f"{processor.audio_tokenizer.num_parameters():,}")  # 10,305,313

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from safetensors.torch import load_file

path = hf_hub_download("gradium/phonon-voices", "voices/LMDIYE0Oa377Qh6Z.safetensors")
voice = load_file(path)["speaker_wavs"][0].T  # (num_frames, 512)

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:
conversation = [
    {"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "audio"}, {"type": "text", "text": "Hello from Phonon."}]}
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    conversation,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    processor_kwargs={"audio_prompt_latents": [voice]},
).to(model.device)
# prompt: <|audio_prompt|> × num_frames, "Hello from Phonon.", <|audio_bos|>

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:
outputs = model.generate(**inputs)  # audio_latents: (batch_size, num_frames, 32)
audio = processor.decode(outputs.audio_latents, outputs.audio_latents_mask)
processor.save_audio(audio, "phonon.wav")

See the docs 🤗 for more!




What's next


Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.
We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.
Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.
Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

summaries.zh: Phonon是一款可在本地设备运行的轻量级文本转语音模型，无需服务器或网络连接，保护用户隐私。该模型支持英语、法语、德语、西班牙语和葡萄牙语，内置超过100种声音，并可通过克隆和设计创建自定义声音。Phonon在Hugging Face Open TTS排行榜上表现优异，尤其在德语和西班牙语中排名第一，并在其他语言中位列前三。模型分为31m和40m两种版本，31m采用Apache 2.0协议免费商用，40m适用于非商业项目。Phonon已支持多种设备平台，包括手机、笔记本电脑、单板计算机和浏览器，并可通过ptts框架实现高效推理。
summaries.en: Phonon is a lightweight, on-device text-to-speech (TTS) model requiring no server or network connection, keeping user data private. Available in 65 MB and 75 MB versions supporting English, French, German, Spanish, and Portuguese, Phonon offers over 100 built-in voices and custom voice creation. It excels in speed and intelligibility on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard, outperforming larger models. The models are licensed under Apache 2.0 (Phonon 31m) for commercial use and CC BY-NC for non-commercial projects. Phonon runs on various devices and browsers, with demos showcasing its offline capabilities. A new inference framework, ptts, supports multiple backends for optimized performance.

items.title: Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out
items.content:
A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

You can try it yourself here.

What the Model Does

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

  • Open: no schema supplied. The model reads the page and works out which parts of it are structured fields (a label followed by a value, a table with a header row over its columns) from context and layout, not from a fixed list of field names, and returns everything it finds as key-value pairs.
  • Schema-directed: you specify the exact shape wanted, field by field, with a type for each one (string, number, or boolean), under the key names your system already uses. Ask for "service_provider" and "client_company", and those are the exact keys that come back. Ask for a table and it fills it row by row, column by column, matching each cell to the key it belongs under. Ask for a field that isn't on the document, and it returns null instead of inventing a value.

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

How It Was Trained

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

  • English multi-domain data: diverse documents collected from the public web, spanning many document types.
  • Brazilian domain data: real Brazilian documents sourced internally, in Portuguese.
  • Multilingual data: a smaller share covering other European and Asian languages, for broader generalization beyond English and Portuguese.

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

Where the Benchmark Draws the Line

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

A Test of Generalization

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

Quality and Cost, at the Same Time

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

Sources

  • BID. Brazilian Identity Document Dataset. Soares, Neves Jr., Bezerra (2020), "BID Dataset: a challenge dataset for document processing tasks," Anais Estendidos XXXIII SIBGRAPI. github.com/ricardobnjunior/Brazilian-Identity-Document-Dataset
  • CORD. Park et al., NAVER CLOVA (2019). huggingface.co/datasets/naver-clova-ix/cord-v2
  • DocVQA. Mathew et al., WACV 2021 (ICDAR 2019). huggingface.co/datasets/lmms-lab/DocVQA
  • WildReceipt. Sun et al., IJCAI 2021. huggingface.co/datasets/Theivaprakasham/wildreceipt
  • SROIE (ICDAR 2019). Held out from training, evaluation only. huggingface.co/datasets/darentang/sroie (mirror); upstream rrc.cvc.uab.es/?ch=13
  • FUNSD. Jaume et al. Held out from training, evaluation only. huggingface.co/datasets/nielsr/funsd (mirror); guillaumejaume.github.io/FUNSD
  • Zenodo Invoices (PT). Cruz & Castelli, NOVA IMS (2022). zenodo.org/records/6371710
  • line_items. Sagarjha456, Hugging Face. huggingface.co/datasets/Sagarjha456/line_items
  • Katanaml Invoices (Donut). Kozłowski & Weichbroth (2021), Mendeley Data doi:10.17632/tnj49gpmtz.2. huggingface.co/datasets/katanaml-org/invoices-donut-data-v1
  • HumynLabs Brazilian Bills and Invoices. huggingface.co/datasets/HumynLabs/Brazilian_Bills_and_Invoices_Dataset
  • Tech4Humans BR-Doc Extraction. huggingface.co/datasets/tech4humans/br-doc-extraction
  • Cardoso, Gabriel Pimenta de Freitas, et al. "DharmaOCR: Specialized Small Language Models for Structured OCR that outperform Open-Source and Commercial Baselines." arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.14314 (2026).

Further Reading

  • How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications
  • Same Cluster, 33 Points More Utilization: What Changed Was the Order
  • GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft
  • Newer Models, Same Advantage

  • Specialization Beats Scale: A Strategic Variable Most AI Procurement Decisions Overlook

summaries.zh: "法域提取器"是一款2亿参数的模型，能从任何文档类型中提取指定字段，输出结构化JSON，成本远低于前沿大语言模型。该模型包含专门用于OCR的DharmaOCR-LITE，可处理合同、发票、身份证件等文档。用户可通过两种方式提取字段：开放式请求（自动识别结构化字段）或基于模式请求（指定字段类型和名称）。模型基于多领域数据训练，无需针对特定类型微调。输出结果为类型化的JSON，可直接用于下游系统。
summaries.en: The Dharma Field Extractor is a 2-billion-parameter model designed to extract specific fields from any document type and output them in structured JSON format. It outperforms general-purpose LLMs in this task while being more cost-effective. The model, built on DharmaOCR-LITE, offers two modes: open, where it identifies and extracts structured fields based on context and layout, and schema-directed, where it follows a predefined schema to extract exact fields with specified types. It supports multiple languages and document types, trained on diverse annotated data. The model returns typed JSON, making it directly usable for downstream systems.

items.title: Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language
items.content:
Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

Why decks are hard for small models

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Build it like a human: a designer and a coder

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

  • The designer reads the plan and writes a structured JSON brief: the palette, the type system, and for each slide its layout, its exact content and a short design rationale.
  • The coder takes one slide's spec from the brief and writes the pptxgenjs JavaScript that draws it, preceded by its reasoning.

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

Synthesizing decks and their reasoning

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

The coder reasons about geometry:

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Steering a deck in plain English

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

## Rollout plan
- March: pilot with two teams
- May: security review complete
- July: rollout to all of engineering
- September: company-wide launch
- November: first adoption review
[[make this a timeline]]

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Category Example directive
Layout [[make this a timeline]]
Tone [[be candid, no spin]]
Audience [[this is for the board]]
Order [[lead with the ask]]
Leaving out [[no pricing]]
Emphasis [[highlight the headline number]]

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Building a check-and-repair harness

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

Evaluation

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

What's next

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

What we learned

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

  1. Put the reasoning in the data. Training on why a choice was made, including what was rejected, teaches more than the choice alone.
  2. Fix the examples before adding a rule. When the teacher got something wrong, our first instinct was to add a rule to its prompt, and that rarely helped. The teacher copied its reference decks far more than it followed instructions, so fixing the reference was what actually changed its output.
  3. Make repairs safe by default. A fix that's kept only when it measurably helps can run on every output.
  4. Build the checker first. It's what makes the data trustworthy and the outputs safe to ship.

summaries.en: Palette teaches a small open-weight model to build custom slide decks in a user's design language by training it on synthetic data and using a human-like designer-coder approach. The model, fine-tuned on the IBM Design Language, ranks first on two domains in PresentBench. It splits tasks: a "designer" creates structured JSON briefs, while a "coder" generates slide code, improving efficiency and consistency. The training data includes synthetic decks with reasoning, addressing small models' weaknesses in layout and decision-making. This method ensures deck ownership and avoids AI defaults while maintaining quality.
